title: BrainGate and the Utah array → Cyberkinetics → Blackrock (and Synchron's public funding)
summary: The Utah Electrode Array was invented at the University of Utah in 1989 and developed with NIH grants; BrainGate grew from federally funded brain-computer interface research at Brown University. Utah spin-off Bionic Technologies was sold to Brown spin-off Cyberkinetics in 2002, which ran the first BrainGate trial from 2004. When Cyberkinetics withdrew, its device manufacturing went to the new company Blackrock Microsystems in 2008, and an academic consortium led by Massachusetts General Hospital took over the trials under a 2009 FDA exemption, funded by federal and philanthropic sources. Blackrock has since received NIH small-business grants. Synchron, a separate company whose Stentrode came from University of Melbourne research, received DARPA/DoD support, and NIH funds a Stentrode trial at Carnegie Mellon. Public BCI research did not end.

links.claim: BrainGate's official history says Cyberkinetics was formed in 2002 as a Brown University spin-off to translate preclinical Brown research into the first BrainGate device. A University of Utah release says Normann's spin-off Bionic Technologies, built on the Utah array, was sold to Cyberkinetics in 2002 and the array was incorporated into BrainGate. License terms were not found.

links.claim: In 2008 Cyberkinetics spun off its device manufacturing, including the Utah array, to new owner Blackrock Microsystems (per BrainGate and Blackrock). This passed the publicly funded technology on through a private sale, not a government transfer; the BrainGate patents went separately to Jeffrey Stibel in 2009.

links.claim: Synchron (not part of the BrainGate chain): Global Venturing reported in 2017 that its Stentrode was developed partly with grants from DoD, DARPA and the Office of Naval Research Global, and that DoD including DARPA took part in its $10 million Series A. NIH (NINDS) funds a Carnegie Mellon early-feasibility trial of the Stentrode BCI (UG3/UH3 NS120191, from 2021).

claims.claim: Public brain-computer interface research was handed over to private companies.
claims.explanation: Federally funded university technology did pass into private spin-offs (Bionic Technologies, Cyberkinetics) and then to Blackrock. But the flow also ran the other way: when Cyberkinetics withdrew, an academic consortium took over the BrainGate trials in 2009, and BrainGate says its research is now funded entirely by federal and philanthropic sources.

claims.claim: Taxpayers funded the development of the Utah array used in BrainGate.
claims.explanation: The University of Utah announced four NIH grants worth about $6.7 million in 2004 to advance the Utah Electrode Array, and BrainGate states the underlying research was funded almost entirely by NIH, the VA and the Department of Defense. Blackrock has also received NIH small-business grants for array development.
